The majority of traffic from the Yandex.Cloud ASN fell into two industry buckets: computer software and gambling. The computer software bucket was predictable for an ASN meant to host third-party applications and software integrations. In fact, we even saw that api.cloudflare.com is a top hostname for Yandex.Cloud request traffic. An overall majority of that traffic succeeded (requests returned 200s) both before and during the event, pointing to legitimate usage.

The gambling sector offers the clearest evidence that malicious automation relocated rather than disappeared. Nearly all of Yandex.Cloud’s bot requests were targeted at one gambling customer account, with traffic shifting among its hostnames. Immediately following the October 8 disruption, bot requests from Yandex.Cloud to this account dropped to zero. Simultaneously, identical requests began appearing from other Russian hosting ASNs, including Radist and Selectel. The incoming traffic maintained an identical fingerprint across providers:

  • The same JA4 TLS client fingerprint
  • The same uncommon request paths and HTTP headers
  • The same custom User-Agent strings

Overall, Russian bot traffic targeting gambling accounts remained essentially flat over the week, moving from 167.7 million to 170.1 million requests (+1.4%). The automation never stopped running; the operators simply migrated their workloads to alternate cloud providers once Yandex.Cloud became unavailable.

Across most industries, the share of bot requests from Yandex.Cloud returning any HTTP 4xx response fell. This is largely due to a drop off in the attack-like traffic mentioned above. This, in combination with the gambling customer analysis, shows that malicious traffic that was sending requests through Yandex.Cloud simply shifted its “services” to other providers after the service disruption.

Finally, when we analyzed social media traffic, we found no unexpected changes in traffic either from Russian-origin IPs (0.6% decrease in total traffic over the event period) or globally (1.2% increase in total traffic over the event period). We repeated the analysis on bot traffic hitting the “post”, “reply”, and “like” endpoints for a specific social media platform and similarly did not find an unexpected shift before or during the event period from either Russian-origin IPs (5.7% decrease in total traffic over the event period) or globally (1.1% increase in total traffic over the event period). Based on our assessment, the data does not appear to support the claims that the strikes crippled social media manipulation, though without further analysis with data outside of Cloudflare, we cannot conclusively say there is no connection.

What the data told us — and what it didn’t

When traffic from Yandex networks collapsed, speculation spread across the Internet that Russian influence operations and malicious botnets had suffered a crippling blow. Cloudflare data tells a different story: across Cloudflare's network, there was no evidence that the strikes knocked social media manipulation offline or otherwise disrupted malicious activity on the Internet. Instead, the data demonstrated:

  • Search indexing dropped. The overwhelming majority of the traffic that dropped from Yandex Search ASN consisted of verified YandexBot crawlers fetching news articles and web assets. The main impact was reduced content discovery in Yandex Search.
  • Malicious automation migrated instead of stopping. While vulnerability scanning and plugin probing temporarily dropped on Yandex.Cloud, high-volume operations quickly moved to alternative hosting networks.

A network disruption means that specific servers stopped sending requests, but it does not mean an automated threat disappeared. Cloud workloads are portable, so when a data center goes dark or an IP prefix gets blocked, operators can migrate their scripts to another provider in hours.

Our analysis here is a reminder that client ASN traffic volume is an unreliable proxy for interpreting automated bot behavior. Defending against automated threats requires inspecting request behavior, such as identifying shared JA4 fingerprints, monitoring anomalous request rates, and applying WAF rules to sensitive endpoints, regardless of which network the request originates from. Physical infrastructure is static, but malicious automation is built to move.

entries.title: Inside Hyperdrive: How we solved a rare Hyperdrive MySQL caching bug
entries.summary: While adding MySQL support to Hyperdrive, we found a subtle protocol bug when caching query results. Here is how we tracked down a 0.001% rate error and made Hyperdrive MySQL generally available.
entries.content:
Hyperdrive support for MySQL is now generally available (GA). Hyperdrive, Cloudflare’s database connection pooler for Workers, initially only supported Postgres. Since we announced the beta for MySQL protocol support last year, we have been working on making our MySQL handling as reliable as our Postgres support.

We’ve learned some things from building and running a MySQL connection pooler on Cloudflare’s network. It turns out that the difference between beta and GA is just 20 bug fixes in a trenchcoat.

During the beta, our goal was to validate that real-world customer usage hit our production availability target of 99.99%. We knew there were gaps in our reliability since we track how often client connections from a Worker end in an error related to Hyperdrive. In addition, we had feedback from customers in the beta that led to the discovery of a rare and subtle bug in our production environment. To convey the complexity of this particular bug, we first need to explain how Hyperdrive works.

What is Hyperdrive?

Hyperdrive is a distributed database connection pooler that connects Cloudflare Workers to SQL databases. Hyperdrive holds warm SQL connections open on our global network and shares these connections across many Worker requests. In addition to connection pooling, Hyperdrive can also cache common queries in our global CDN cache, reducing latency and load on the origin database.

Establishing a connection to a SQL database is expensive, taking a minimum of five network round trips. On a serverless compute platform like Workers, establishing a connection for each request would be impractical, both because of the amount of latency added to each request, but also because a large number of open connections can incur high per-connection resource costs. While MySQL fares better here than Postgres since MySQL doesn’t use an entire OS process per connection, a typical deployment can still run into resource issues with a large number of connections.

For more details, see our blog post introducing Hyperdrive.

A journey to stability

Some of the issues we ran into were small and easy to fix once reported. One of the first problems reported in the beta was that emojis written to the database were not being correctly returned. This was a bug related to character set encoding. Hyperdrive negotiates the encoding for the connection in the startup handshake and we negotiate 

utf8
 as the encoding. As it turns out, 
utf8
 is a deprecated alias for 
utf8mb3
 which is not all of UTF-8: it only supports 1-3 bytes per Unicode code point, while full UTF-8 has a max of 4 bytes per code point. To get all of UTF-8, we needed to change our handshake to use 
utf8mb4
 , which fixed the emoji issue.

Another encoding-related bug occurred when we added connection cleanup via COM_RESET_CONNECTION. This is a lightweight MySQL command to clear any session state in a given connection, which is exactly what Hyperdrive needs to ensure that no session-level state leaks between checkouts. But adding this connection cleanup step caused encoding issues once again! It turns out that COM_RESET_CONNECTION does not reset the connection state to the character set encoding we negotiated at connection startup; it instead resets the connection to the server default. This means that after negotiating utf8mb4 on a MySQL server instance that defaults to 

latin1
, once we run COM_RESET_CONNECTION, our connection now has an encoding of 
latin1
. The fix is to always run a command setting the encoding to utf8mb4 after a connection reset.

A hard-to-find bug

During the beta, our highest-volume MySQL customer reported a small but consistent rate of empty query responses for which a non-empty response was always expected. We started the investigation by combing through all of our telemetry and understanding the user’s logic. Then we also increased the trace rate for this Hyperdrive instance, hoping to see the execution flow of this bug. We searched for network issues that could explain the issue — but nothing seemed to account for this behavior. This error occurred about 0.001% of the time, which made it very hard to find relevant end-to-end execution traces.

But we did have one clue: the bug only occurred on Hyperdrive instances with caching enabled. This made us suspect an issue with Hyperdrive’s MySQL caching.

Hyperdrive caching

To understand Hyperdrive's caching, we first need to talk about Hyperdrive's topology and how it interacts with the CDN cache. Every Hyperdrive instance has a split architecture with two nodes: a Client and an Endpoint. The Client node runs on the same machine as the user’s Worker, handles local caching (if enabled), and forwards queries to the Endpoint if needed. The Endpoint node holds the connection pool and is placed in the data center closest to the origin database. Each node uses the Cloudflare CDN cache local to the data center it is running in. Importantly, this means that if the two nodes are running in the same data center, they will share a cache.

Sharing the cache between Client and Endpoint is generally good for performance. We use a hash of the contents of the query’s wire messages with some normalization and store the result bytes in the cache. If a Hyperdrive Client running in the same data center as its Endpoint receives a request, and that Endpoint has recently cached the results of the same query, the Client can serve the response directly from the shared data center cache. To work correctly, this scheme requires that the same bytes are cached for the same response, whether stored by the Client or the Endpoint.

MySQL client/server protocol

Since we couldn’t get a direct trace of the issue, we decided to spend time looking at the MySQL client / server protocol. Perhaps we had an assumption about Postgres’ protocol built into our MySQL handling that was causing these issues.

The protocol describes how a MySQL client communicates with a MySQL server. This can be somewhat confusing in the case of database connection pooling since we have two components acting like clients and two acting like servers. The first client is the Worker using a MySQL client library, and it connects to the first component acting like a server, the Hyperdrive Client. The Hyperdrive Client connects to the Hyperdrive Endpoint which acts as a MySQL client connecting to the actual MySQL origin server.

This protocol starts with the Connection Phase where the MySQL client and the MySQL server agree upon a common authentication method and capabilities. Once a connection is established, the client and server begin the Command Phase, where the client sends commands (e.g. SQL statements) to be executed with the server responding and waiting for the next command.

Capabilities are exchanged during the Connection Phase to support protocol evolution while remaining backwards compatible. Each capability is a feature, like supporting compression during the Command Phase. The clients and servers must only use features which the other supports, otherwise a protocol desync can occur, leading to unexpected behavior.

This capability negotiation can be tricky for Hyperdrive, since Hyperdrive acts as a client to the origin database, and acts as a server to the Worker. To ensure that Hyperdrive can parse the messages from the origin MySQL server, Hyperdrive has a fixed set of capability flags which are used to communicate to the origin database. Since it is possible for Hyperdrive’s set of capabilities to be different from the Worker client’s set of capabilities, Hyperdrive needs to translate all origin responses encoded by its capabilities to the capabilities that the Worker expects.

While trying to debug this issue, we found that a popular MySQL client library for Node.js (

mysql2
) does not currently support the CLIENT_DEPRECATE_EOF capability, which changes how result sets are terminated. Without this capability, the server sends an EOF packet between the column definitions and rows, then another EOF packet at the end of the result set. When CLIENT_DEPRECATE_EOF is negotiated, the metadata EOF packet is omitted and the final EOF packet is replaced with an OK packet. MySQL server 5.7.5 and later supports this capability, but the newer OK-packet behavior is only used when the client negotiates it.

While Hyperdrive does support the CLIENT_DEPRECATE_EOF capability, it’s possible that the Worker’s MySQL driver does not. To handle this, Hyperdrive adjusts its behavior to support the capabilities that the Worker client driver expects. This means rewriting result sets to include EOFs and to translate all OK packets to EOFs when required.

After days of looking through telemetry, documentation, and Hyperdrive code, everything clicked. We finally came across the last missing piece: a faulty assumption in our Hyperdrive Client caching code. We baked in an assumption when implementing the Client caching for Postgres: that we can cache exactly the bytes we wrote back to the Worker. While this was a reasonable assumption to make with Postgres’ wire protocol, it no longer holds due to the mismatch in MySQL capabilities. If a Client node is caching exactly what it writes back to the Worker, these bytes are in a different format than what an Endpoint node would be expecting. That’s because the Endpoint node is always working with Hyperdrive’s capabilities, while the Client node writes back bytes that are translated to match the Worker’s capabilities.

Now if we put all these clues together, we can understand scenarios where Hyperdrive can return a MySQL response encoded with the wrong capabilities, leading to the unexpected empty results and hangs. The bug occurs when both the Client and Endpoint are in the same data center, sharing a cache, and when one reads a value cached by the other.

Here’s a closer look at two such scenarios.

Endpoint caches, Client reads

  • The Endpoint is in the middle of servicing a request for query Q. It gets back a response R from the origin server and caches response result bytes R_hyperdrive (Response encoded with Hyperdrive capabilities) into the shared cache.
  • Client receives another request for query Q, checks the shared cache and finds R_hyperdrive.
  • Client responds to the Worker with R_hyperdrive without translating to the Worker’s capabilities.

This diagram shows that flow:

Client caches, Endpoint reads

  • Client is finishing serving a request for query Q, and it writes the translated response bytes R_worker to cache.
  • Endpoint is in the middle of servicing a request for Q, and checks the cache to find R_worker.
  • Endpoint sends R_worker to a different Client, and this Client tries to translate R_worker to the Worker’s capabilities, and ends up sending an early EOF or hangs.

You can see that here:

Once we found this type of failure mode, the fix was simple. We now make sure that we always write back a canonical version of the query result bytes in the cache encoded using Hyperdrive’s capabilities, no matter which node stored it. After releasing this change, the empty row problem went away — and our success rate for Client connections reached 99.99%.

Reliability is a feature

You can use Hyperdrive support for MySQL today! Create a Hyperdrive to an existing MySQL-compatible database via the dashboard or wrangler, or connect to a new PlanetScale database. If you run into any issues or have questions, reach out on our Discord. 

      
npx wrangler hyperdrive create HYPERDRIVE_NAME --connection-string="mysql://user:password@db-host.example.com:3306/dbname"

entries.title: Under the hood, off the hot path: How D1 scales to millions of databases
entries.summary: A deep dive into how D1 architected its control plane to scale and manage millions of databases, while keeping data plane query operations at the edge. We share guiding principles on how to build on the Developer Platform effectively.
entries.content:
Traditional database architecture assumes you have one or two big database clusters per application, usually accompanied by a connection pooling solution. AI-assisted development and vibe coding platforms turn this model inside out and are driving applications toward many small databases: one per user, application, preview environment, or tenant.

That model fits D1 particularly well. D1 is Cloudflare's managed, serverless database based on SQLite. It allows you to create millions of databases and only pay for what you use.

The question becomes: how do you scale the control plane for millions of databases without making every query slower by sending it through centralized bottlenecks?

We made a lot of architectural changes to scale out D1 to support platforms with millions of created databases, hundreds of thousands of which are active at any point.

This post is a behind-the-scenes deep dive into how the D1 control plane works. Many of the architectural patterns we will describe can be used by anyone building on top of Cloudflare’s Developer Platform. The post also gives a glimpse into how we build our own control planes.

Growth in numbers

There was already a steady growth in D1 usage when we started planning these changes, but we knew we would need to support a much bigger scale once large platforms started building with D1.

Here is how things have played out so far.

D1 has seen a 15x growth in the number of live non-deleted databases over the past one year, and a 65x growth over the past 2 years (as of October 8, 2026).

We have also seen 18x growth in the number of daily active databases over the past year (as of October 8, 2026). A database is considered active if it executed at least one query during that day.

Established and successful platforms are already building with D1, using the same tools available to all Cloudflare users.

"ChatGPT Sites lets anyone turn ideas into shareable experiences. D1 gives our users a simple, scalable way to add features like custom metrics, leaderboards, and comments to their dashboards, games, and tools."

- Jon Abrams, ChatGPT Sites @ OpenAI

While we were making the changes described in this blog post, we periodically load-tested against a target well above our expected growth. This guided where to focus our optimization efforts.

Guiding engineering principles

Applications built on the Cloudflare Developer Platform range from full-stack applications to service APIs, from internal single-user portals to massive multi-tenant vibe coding platforms, and everything in between.

While building out the D1 control plane to support millions of databases, the following tenets and principles were guiding our architecture decisions and are useful for anyone building their control and data planes on our platform.

  • Design all processes with failure and idempotency in mind. Failures will happen, so the system needs to self-correct where possible and continue making progress.
  • Avoid centralized single-region components in any hot path for data plane operations (in our case all query requests).
  • Use Workers KV, a globally distributed KV store, for critical routing metadata so that cache misses only rarely need to query central databases.
  • Use Hyperdrive to access central Postgres databases for efficient connection pooling and optimized routing and caching, using read replicas wherever possible.
  • Periodically precompute aggregations in the database to avoid scan queries during user request processing.
  • Use eventual consistency and queuing between components that don’t need strong consistency to increase reliability and availability.
  • Load-test the application with realistic workloads to discover bottlenecks and inefficiencies, and focus on optimizing those first.

There are more engineering principles we follow internally to build our systems, but the above are generic enough and apply to anyone building on Cloudflare.

The following sections will dive into the main system components and processes of the D1 control plane regarding the lifecycle of a D1 database, and showcase how to put these principles into practice with a real-world system.

High-level architecture

Let’s start off by introducing the main components of D1.

There are a few more arrows and boxes missing from the diagram for secondary processes supporting D1, but these are the ones providing D1’s public feature set. We will explore the rest in dedicated sections in the rest of the blog post.

First of all, each D1 database is backed by one SQLite Durable Object, which makes it very easy to create millions of them.

The “HTTP API” shape represents all our API surfaces including the Cloudflare dashboard, Wrangler, and Cloudflare CLI. All API requests go through Cloudflare’s edge gateway and are served by the D1 Edge API Worker.

The diagram shows the HTTP endpoints that allow users to execute SQL queries against their databases as the “Query endpoints”. The remaining endpoints include the usual database operations like creating, deleting, and listing databases, along with import/export and time travel features. These are shown as the “CRUD endpoints”.

The CRUD endpoints use Hyperdrive to query a Postgres cluster in our central data centers (referred to as “Core”). There are two configurations. One configuration has caching enabled and targets the Postgres read replicas. The other configuration has caching disabled and targets the Postgres primary.

The Edge API Worker might invoke the D1 Eyeball Worker (depending on the type of request). The Eyeball Worker is our proxy for all requests that need to be handled by the underlying D1 Durable Objects (DO). This allows us to put all query handling inside the Eyeball Worker, including observability, automatic retries, error handling, and other query-specific behaviors.

Workers KV acts as our caching layer at the edge for read-heavy metadata and can be read by all the D1 Workers.

The “Worker Binding” shape represents all users’ Workers with a D1 Worker binding. Requests from the D1 Binding go directly to the D1 Eyeball Worker, which in turn forwards the request to the Durable Object backing the database and proxies the response back to the User Worker.

We have two methods for users to execute queries in their databases. One is over the HTTP API query endpoints, and the other is through a Worker they deploy in their accounts with a D1 Binding.

In terms of operations, we fold each operation into one of the following categories:

  • Data plane: any database query related request; should be as fast as possible and always at the edge.
  • Control plane: any HTTP API operation or internal flows that run in response to a non-query user request; they can depend on central single-region components.
  • Background asynchronous plane: any analytical and billing-related workflow; can be eventually consistent and runs anywhere.

There is a lot more under the hood, so let’s dive into the key flows.

Fast on-demand database creation close to the user

Multi-tenant platforms and AI agent-driven development require creating a lot of database instances in a fast, cost-efficient, and reliable way.

The following is an example Wrangler command to create a D1 database:

      
% time wrangler d1 create "demo-01"

✅ Successfully created DB 'demo-01' in region WEUR
...
0.56s user 0.13s system 42% cpu 1.614 total

When a user creates a D1 database, several things need to happen before the database is ready to receive queries.

  • Check that the account can create more databases against the free tier limit or its account limits.
  • Generate a unique D1 database UUID, a unique Durable Object ID (
    newUniqueId()
    ), and initialize the underlying Durable Object (DO) with the account and database information.
  • Persist the newly created database’s information in Postgres (one row per database, including metadata and the mapping to the initialized Durable Object ID).
  • Write the mapping from a database ID to the Durable Object ID in Workers KV (later used by the data plane and the query endpoints).

Let’s examine the actual flow and how we recover from failures at each step.

Once a database creation request comes in, our Edge API Worker handler is invoked in the nearest Cloudflare location at the edge. Edge API queries our Postgres read replicas over Hyperdrive with caching enabled (with cache TTL of a few seconds) to get the number of non-deleted databases for the given account.

The Edge API Worker forwards control plane requests to data centers near our Postgres cluster for endpoints that do multiple round-trips to Postgres (step 2), and the “create database” endpoint is one of them. The reason is that a round-trip from afar can be hundreds of milliseconds, whereas being near Postgres can be a few milliseconds. For endpoints that do at most one Postgres query we don’t need to do this optimization since Hyperdrive already handles efficient routing through the Cloudflare network.

Creating a D1 database without any options places the database near the request’s location by default. You can influence the location of the database by providing an explicit location hint or a jurisdiction. The location hints and jurisdiction options are identical to what Durable Objects support, so when these are provided they are just passed straight through to the underlying Durable Object initialization.

With the default creation we want the D1 databases to be created near the original location of the request, close to the user. To achieve this, during step 4 of the diagram, we internally forward the request execution to a data center close to the original request’s location and invoke the underlying Durable Object from there. This ensures that the underlying Durable Object is placed near the user.

You can implement similar routing techniques by using explicit Worker placement hints and at runtime invoking the right Worker via Service Bindings.

The creation endpoint is a bit of a weird case in terms of placement because even though we query Postgres at least two times, we also do a long-distance call to the underlying Durable Objects, which differ per request, so running the request to either side of the world could be inefficient. That's why we leaned towards forwarding the initial request near Postgres.

The next step is to generate the database UUID along with a new unique Durable Object ID using the 

newUniqueId()
 API and invoke the 
init(options)
 RPC function on the new Durable Object’s stub. The Durable Object stores the information in its durable storage so that every incoming request from that point on has all the metadata for the linked database.

Once the Edge API Worker gets the initialization response, it persists the database metadata into our central Postgres primary database over Hyperdrive, one metadata row per database.

The steps above are wrapped in a retry loop (steps 5-7 in the diagram). When the DO initialization or the write to Postgres fails we retry with different IDs (this is important, as we will see in the next section).

The write to Postgres is the “creation checkpoint” where a database is considered created even if the final response fails to reach the user. The database from that point on is included in all the control plane operations and can be bound to a Worker to serve queries.

At this point the D1 database is ready to receive queries.

The final creation confirmation RPC to the Durable Object happens in a 

waitUntil()
and is OK to fail. This call signals the DO that the database is now active, and the DO updates Workers KV with the database metadata so that any subsequent query can immediately read the information from Workers KV cache without needing to query Postgres.

A common question is why can’t the creation flow run entirely inside a Postgres transaction to simplify the process? The answer is simply that it cannot scale, since it leads to connections being held while the Durable Object is being initialized, which could be on the other side of the world.

Heartbeats for self-correcting databases

Each D1 Durable Object periodically heartbeats the control plane to get the latest database state (active or deleted) and account limits (more on this in the enforcement sections later). The interval is 30 seconds with a per-database jitter on top. We also have knobs to change the interval by database or account, or disable heartbeats entirely.

Heartbeats can tolerate slightly out-of-date data, meaning they can be served by Hyperdrive’s multiple caching layers or by a Postgres read replica. This heartbeat flow enables the Durable Object to self-correct to reflect the source of truth (Postgres) regarding the creation and deletion of databases.

One clarifying detail before we move on. The reason we use different database UUID and Durable Object IDs for each retry in the creation flow of the previous section (step 5) is that if we reused the database UUIDs with fresh Durable Object IDs, multiple Durable Objects would think they own the same database leading to difficult-to-debug situations. The periodic heartbeats also act as a cleanup for orphaned objects.

Also, it’s important that we first initialize the Durable Object before we persist the database mapping in Postgres, otherwise query requests could start to flow to the Durable Object and would be rejected due to uninitialized state.

For example, let’s assume the following failure scenario and why it is self-correcting:

  • We executed everything from the previous section until we initialized Durable Object A, and then, the write to Postgres fails.
  • The Worker retries the loop and initializes a new DO with a different ID B, and this time it persists to Postgres.
  • We now have two Durable Objects initialized and running as part of this request, but only one of them is valid.
  • The user can only query Durable Object B because that’s the only ID available in Postgres, which is our source of truth.
  • Within 30 seconds, DO A sends its next heartbeat to the control plane and receives back a response that its database does not exist. This will trigger DO A to mark itself as deleted.

A similar flow happens for the deletion endpoint.

Another self-correcting behavior of the heartbeats is making sure the Workers KV data eventually reflects reality: whether a database is active or deleted.

The final step of the creation flow to update Workers KV is “best-effort” and can fail without causing problems. It’s eventually consistent, and the next time the Durable Object heartbeats it will ensure that the Workers KV item has been written with the correct value. Since Workers KV is eventually consistent without a way to do a consistent read, the Durable Object acts as the serialization point for the writes to the Workers KV items.

Deletion works the same way in reverse: the Durable Object owns writing its “deleted” state to Workers KV, again best-effort during the actual deletion operation, and if that fails the heartbeat will correct it eventually. The Durable Object stores the active or deleted state in its storage too, so it can reject or accept query requests immediately, even if Workers KV is stale and allows requests through.

Overall, the database heartbeats are the fallback mechanism for getting into a consistent state when operations need to write into an external datastore and also update the Durable Object itself.

Decoupling the hot path: keeping queries off the central database

The key principle for query endpoints is to avoid talking to Postgres or any other centralized single-region component. Each query request over HTTP executes our Edge API Worker close to the original user request location, and then goes straight to the D1 Durable Object via the Eyeball Worker.

The Edge API Worker is responsible for doing standard HTTP API authentication, resource-based authorization, rate limiting at the account and database level, request validation, checking the entitlements of the account, and other API-related functions before executing the actual business logic.

The Eyeball Worker, on the other hand, skips these extra checks (apart from its own dedicated rate limiting), since under the hood, a D1 Binding is a Service Binding to the D1 Eyeball Worker. Each user Worker’s D1 Binding carries encoded information that authorizes access to one specific D1 database that the D1 Eyeball Worker validates and allows the request through.

The following diagram shows the execution of a query through the HTTP API.

  • A user sends a query request over the HTTP API.
  • The Edge API Worker first tries to load the mapping from a D1 UUID to the database metadata from Workers KV.
  • In rare cases, the item cannot be found in Workers KV, either because the write failed as described earlier or potentially due to an availability issue. We then fall back to reading the mapping from Hyperdrive targeting the Postgres replicas. Before querying the actual replicas, Hyperdrive first checks its cache in the caller location, then its cache near the Postgres cluster location, and only if both are cache misses queries the Postgres replicas for the mapping.
  • Once we have the mapping, the Edge API Worker calls the Eyeball Worker over Worker Service Bindings passing the relevant IDs.
  • The Eyeball Worker does its validation and forwards the query request to the D1 Durable Object.
  • The D1 Durable Object executes the SQL query and returns the result through Eyeball Worker to the Edge API Worker, which returns it back to the user.
      
// Edge API Worker
const parsed = parseQueries(request);

const cachedDB = await withRetries(getCachedDatabase(parsed.dbUuid));

const response = await env.EYEBALL_WORKER.query({
  db: cachedDB,
  queries: parsed.queries,
});

return response;

If you are wondering why we use 

newUniqueId()
 during the database creation rather than addressing Durable Objects by “name” to eliminate steps 2 and 3 above, the answer is to avoid a lookup round-trip to a central mapping of “name” to “Durable Object ID” during query requests. The Durable Object ID alone would not be enough, since we also need other metadata to help us pick the right Durable Object Namespace to use in our Eyeball Worker. Hence, we would replace one lookup with two.

In most cases, even with many of our own applications, addressing Durable Objects by name works great, and it removes the need for a lookup from your own IDs to a Durable Object ID, so use that as a starting point and only move to unique DO IDs if you have to.

You might also wonder why we use Workers KV when we already have Hyperdrive Caching.

Workers KV is a durable datastore, not just a cache: if an item falls out of KV's edge cache, the read is served from KV's own storage rather than Postgres, keeping Postgres out of the data plane. In a catastrophic cache purge scenario, a million databases trying to fetch their routing information would lead to metastable failures.

As a reminder, query requests from a user Worker with a D1 Binding do not need to resolve the D1 UUID mapping metadata because the binding itself holds that information internally, so requests go straight to the Eyeball Worker and the Durable Object.

For the query execution itself and how Durable Objects are implemented under the hood, read our blog post about D1 read replication that dives into all the nitty-gritty details.

Next, let's look at the asynchronous processes that support D1.

Enforcing storage usage limits

All platforms that reach a certain scale eventually need to enforce billing and usage limits. At the time of writing, D1 has a 5 GB per-account storage limit on the Free plan and 1 TB on Workers Paid (can be raised on request).

In general, usage limit enforcement and billing systems are good candidates for eventual consistency and asynchronous processing, and in the following sections we will explore how D1 implements the enforcement of these limits.

Asynchronous update processing with queues

The first step of the journey is that each Durable Object publishes storage usage updates to a Kafka-like queue for batching and asynchronous processing. The control plane does not need to process every update synchronously: it is fine if a load spike is not reflected immediately and our usage information is stale. The important thing is that it cannot overload Postgres and impact users of D1. We ensure this by limiting the number of queue consumers, and therefore the write load on Postgres.

The queue consumer system runs inside Cloudflare’s central data centers (“Core”), whereas the Durable Objects themselves are spread everywhere in the world at the edge. The usage is aggregated locally per edge server and then published into the internal queue system.

The guiding principle here is that we use a queue to smooth out and batch writes to our central regional Postgres data store.

Batching usage deltas and pre-aggregations

The queue consumer writes the latest reported size for each database into a Postgres table. This isn’t what we need for enforcement decisions though. For enforcement decisions, we need the sum of all storage usage across the whole account. When we come to read the usage at enforcement time, we can’t afford to run 

SELECT sum(storage) FROM database_stats WHERE account_id = ?
. The cost of this query scales linearly with the number of databases on each account. This doesn’t scale for accounts with millions of D1 databases, like some of the agentic coding platforms built with D1.

Ideally, we want a lookup table that will allow us to go directly from account ID to total database storage. The solution is to use incremental view maintenance to precompute the total, and keep it up to date when we have database storage changes.

Let’s call this table 

account_database_stats
.

In theory, we could make the queue consumer update 

database_stats
 and 
account_database_stats
 itself for every update that comes in. In practice, this would end up with a lot of write lock contention on a single row for large accounts. Instead, we add a third table called 
account_database_stats_changes
 that acts like a queue of changes. This is a log of all changes, and can have multiple entries per account. We then periodically aggregate updates from that table into 
account_database_stats
. The flow looks like this:
  • The queue consumer writes usage info to the 
    database_stats
     table for a specific database.
  • A trigger calculates the difference in storage for that database and puts the delta in an 
    account_database_stats_changes
     table (one row per delta).
  • A scheduled job runs every second to consume everything in 
    account_database_stats_changes
     and update 
    account_database_stats
     with the sum of those deltas.

Concretely, the scheduled job runs this query:

      
WITH updates AS MATERIALIZED (
  DELETE FROM account_database_stats_changes
  RETURNING *
),
changes AS MATERIALIZED (
  SELECT
    account_id,
    SUM(storage_change) AS storage
  FROM updates
  GROUP BY account_id
)
INSERT INTO account_database_stats (account_id, storage)
SELECT
  account_id,
  storage
FROM changes
ON CONFLICT (account_id) DO UPDATE
SET storage = account_database_stats.storage + EXCLUDED.storage;

It gets a list of updates from 

account_database_stats_changes
, aggregates them by account, and then writes the deltas to the per-account table. This avoids write contention on any particular row, because we aggregate the changes before writing them.

The Common Table Expression (CTE) 

DELETE ... RETURNING
 atomically consumes the pending changes and passes the deleted rows to the next CTE. Postgres executes the data-modifying CTE exactly once and to completion. The query then groups those changes by account and applies one aggregated update per account, reducing write contention.

This schema design is a pattern used by many other Cloudflare teams, and it lets us scale to millions of resources per account without each additional resource making common operations more expensive.

It’s worth noting that the total is eventually consistent. It’s not like first-class incremental view maintenance that you find in some other databases. We are already using a queue to get the updates from the Durable Objects into Postgres, so we are already fine with eventual consistency.

Cached reads via Hyperdrive

We now have a lookup table for each account’s total storage. What next?

Each D1 Durable Object periodically retrieves the account’s usage through the periodic heartbeat we mentioned earlier. We query Postgres with  

SELECT storage FROM account_database_stats WHERE account_id = ?
 and compare that to the account’s entitlement and tier limits. If the total is over the limit then we forbid all writes that would increase the database size.

The query goes to Postgres replicas through Hyperdrive, and uses Hyperdrive’s built-in cache. Hyperdrive’s cache key is made up of the query and all parameter values, with the expiration time-to-live being a few seconds. By using the account ID as the only parameter, every database on that account will share the same cached value, which is what we want.

Time for a neat cache trick. Cached reads via Hyperdrive by default have a 60s expiration, and the Hyperdrive cache configuration applies to all queries. For specific queries we want cached values with lower expiration time. By adding a 

dynamic_ttl
 parameter to the query we generate a different cache key every X seconds, therefore reading fresh values sooner. 
      
-- $2 = Math.floor(Date.now() / (X * 1000))
SELECT storage, $2 as dynamic_ttl
FROM account_database_stats WHERE account_id = $1

It might be tempting to make a query that takes account ID and database ID as parameters. That would let you find the account total and subtract the total for the current database. That would get an exact answer to the question “how much storage is this database allowed to use before we start enforcing?”, which would allow the database to start enforcing limits earlier.

Doing this would mean that the database ID would be included in Hyperdrive’s cache key, which would make cache hit rates very poor. For accounts with millions of active databases, an account-based cache key means that most of the heartbeats use the same cached account information from Hyperdrive and never reach Postgres.

Limit enforcement is slightly slower than it could be in terms of reaction to usage changes, but this is acceptable.

Separately from the above flow, we have a process that periodically snapshots the storage usage information from Postgres into a ClickHouse cluster, so that we can get a historical view of storage over time. These ClickHouse events are also the source of truth for storage usage billing purposes.

Enforcing row usage limits at the edge

D1 also enforces daily execution usage limits for free tier customers. The pattern we use here is different, and is worth mentioning as well.

Whenever an SQL query is executed in a Durable Object, we track how many rows it reads and writes (including index updates if needed) to perform the query. When the query execution completes, we publish a usage event that ends up in another ClickHouse cluster. These events are what drive our row-based usage billing.

A central component, call it “Limiter”, runs in our Core data centers and periodically queries the usage events from ClickHouse since the start of the day:

      
SELECT account_id, sum(rows_read) as reads, sum(rows_written) as writes
FROM requests
WHERE timestamp > toStartOfDay(now())
GROUP BY account_id HAVING reads > ? or writes > ?

ClickHouse deals with this kind of query better than Postgres, and we also benefit from not overloading our Postgres cluster for analytical queries.

For every account that is over the limit, we check their entitlements and tier (this limit applies only to free tier users). If they are over a limit, we email them (deduplicated throughout the day), and set a key in Quicksilver, our internal globally distributed key-value store with fast sub-second replication, with an expiry date at the end of the day. If the account upgrades to the Workers Paid tier, we receive a message on a queue and clear the Quicksilver key.

Each D1 Durable Object periodically checks Quicksilver at the edge to find out whether its account has been limited, and in case it is, they reject any future query execution until the limit is lifted.

Someone building on the Developer Platform can use Workers KV Instant, which is built on top of Quicksilver.

This pattern avoids any load into the regional Postgres for the entire flow and uses the right tool for the right job. Doing analytics queries with ClickHouse is more efficient than doing them in Postgres.

This pattern is common across the company, but different from the approach we use for storage usage limit enforcement. In the future, we may migrate other limit enforcements to use this pattern instead.

Conclusion

The D1 architecture is designed around separating control plane concerns from hot-path query execution.

Each decision follows our guiding principles: reducing central regional bottlenecks, using caching and read replicas along with eventual consistency when possible to scale out read throughput, and choosing the right data store for each job: Postgres for transactional metadata, ClickHouse for analytics, and Workers KV for globally replicated routing data.

If you are building a vibe coding platform and want to offer your users managed SQLite databases in a fast, cost-efficient, and reliable way, consider using D1.

If you are building applications on Workers and the Developer Platform, the patterns and trade-offs covered here reflect real decisions made for D1. Use them as a foundation in your own applications.

Check out the D1 documentation, and let us know what you build in the D1 Discord channel!

Acknowledgements

Massive thanks to Cloudflare’s internal Databases and Hyperdrive teams, who helped us find problematic usage patterns and suggested improvements.

entries.title: Rewinding the exponential: How we keep hardware usage down
entries.summary: Our strategies to optimize our data pipeline throughput without compromising data quality.
entries.content:
More than 20% of the web sits behind Cloudflare’s network, and our team, the Data team, owns the data pipeline responsible for plumbing that data (and more) from our global network to applicable central data centers. The Cloudflare network is a globally distributed system supporting tens of thousands of servers. Data that power Cloudflare Logs, SQL API, observability, internal analytics, and more flow through this network and use our data pipeline to serve customers.

In May of this year, we were providing data delivery at roughly two billion events per second. This includes customer traffic as well as data sent from internal teams. Year after year, we tackle the same problem — exponential traffic growth against linear hardware growth. We have to react to this increase in order to keep resource costs under control. Over the past five years, we’ve made various improvements to compensate for the data volume increase in comparison to hardware allocation, equivalent to deferring two and a half years of hardware expansion. This post details those changes: breaking up our monolithic data schema in 2022, adjusting compression in 2024, rearchitecting pipeline replication in spring 2026, decentralizing sampling in summer 2026, and introducing aggregations into the pipeline in fall 2026.

Background

Our pipeline starts with an internal service called Logfwdr, where we collect from highly distributed data sources (think: Workers, FL). We then feed this data to a set of centralized receivers, which eventually push them onto our buffering system, Buftee. Consumers fetch data from Buftee and distribute data to their final destinations, like ClickHouse, which we rely on heavily.

Unpacking the monolith

In 2022, we dismantled our one and only schema. Previously, there was a single stream packed with every product's fields, forcing Cloudflare-internal consumers to ingest everything and demux or discard records via filters. At the time, most of Cloudflare’s data products were built on HTTP, Security and CDN metadata. In 2021, our message schema looked like this:

Some fields here belonged under the same product, but some were completely irrelevant to each other. The hypothesis was that none of these teams require 100% of fields in the monolithic schema. In other words, we can create small messages for each product’s required fields. Although we were going to duplicate fields, some of them in every message, replacing this firehose with product-specific schemas actually reduced the backbone bandwidth usage by 35-40%, knocking out roughly a year’s worth of compressed traffic growth.

Compression

By 2024, as traffic steadily grew, we were tackling network congestion issues on a daily basis. To react to this, we changed our compression algorithm from LZ4 to zstd. We had already experimented with zstd compression before, but we noticed a higher CPU usage at the time. Therefore, we were careful to track the metrics to ensure the trade-off was worth it.

Initially, we rolled this change out to a few servers. To our relief, we didn’t observe a noticeable difference in CPU usage.

With more confidence, we gradually rolled out to our entire fleet, which also showed little impact to CPUs. In the end, there was nearly a 40% reduction in compressed traffic throughput. The uncompressed bytes remained at the same growth, meaning we could support more than 1.5x the amount of traffic with the same size pipe. Or another way to put it, the estimated growth-equivalent reductions put us at about 10 months prior.

Now, in 2026, we attempted three strategies to reduce uncompressed bytes (and thus, compressed bytes).

Load balancing

To make analytics resilient against regional disasters, our systems require redundant data to be stored in multiple centralized regions (data subject to Customer Metadata Boundaries is stored strictly within its designated region). Historically, the simplest way to achieve disaster resilience was double-writing: Logfwdr transmitted two full copies of every non-regional analytics event — one to each centralized region. Each region then independently processed a complete copy through to ClickHouse. We also apply sampling in each region, an incredibly scalable technique that works for all volumes of data during any traffic conditions. We downsample high-volume traffic while rare events are preserved.

This infrastructure was manageable when only a handful of streams used secondary regions. However, as we expanded disaster resilience across almost all analytics streams, Logfwdr traffic doubled across the board. Sending every event, twice, over wide-area transit was unsustainable against our exponential traffic growth.

We had already tackled a similar challenge for Logpush. For Logpush, Logfwdr treats the centralized data centers as a unified, shared pool of receivers: each message is sent to only one region, failing over to another destination if a machine or facility is unreachable. That model had already proven its worth during large incidents, shifting traffic seamlessly from one location to another without human intervention. This automatic failover was possible because Logpush delivery is stateless, as customer destinations do not care which centralized data center pushes the logs.

Analytics was trickier. Unlike stateless logs, ClickHouse clusters in both regions still need a full copy of non-regional data to allow instant, independent query failover. The breakthrough was decoupling pipeline transit from database redundancy:

1. Shared Ingest Pool: We adopted Logpush’s model to the analytics streams. Logfwdr dispatches each event exactly once across wide-area transit to whichever centralized receiver is available.

2. Late Replication from centralized regions: Instead of replicating traffic at source, replication happens as late as possible in the pipeline. Data lands in our distributed buffering layer, Buftee, and remote inserters stream cross-data-center copies downstream.

3. Resilient Failure Handling: If a centralized region goes down, Logfwdrs immediately routes all non-regional traffic to the surviving region. If the inter-data center connection blips, each cluster continues ingesting its local share without backpressure; remote inserters catch up from Buftee's retention buffer once the backbone recovers.

For the datasets we migrated, the cutover eliminated approximately 43 GB/s of compressed transit traffic while adding only ~7 GB/s of cross-data-center replication on our pipeline. Two architectural factors explain this asymmetry:

1. Replication happens downstream of sampling: In the old model, Logfwdrs transmitted two copies of raw, unsampled events over wide-area transit. In the new model, Logfwdrs send a single copy to centralized receivers, which immediately apply sampling before buffering into Buftee, carrying only this already-compacted stream.

2. Better compression through uniform partitioning: Data at source is fragmented across thousands of individual servers. After centralization, streams are aggregated and partitioned into uniform batches over wider time windows. This structural uniformity allows compression algorithms to achieve dramatically higher compression ratios than Logfwdr transit batches ever could.

Overall, this was a net reduction of 36 GB/s across wide-area networks. We rolled this out initially to two datasets, HTTP analytics and Ready-Analytics, our in-house one-click analytics product.

We’ve been actively migrating more datasets to this load-balanced architecture since the spring.

Sampling from the get-go

Another strategy we employed was further expanding our sampling mechanism so that we pulled critical processing earlier into the pipeline. Sampling was already used in our centralized services, particularly the receivers, easing pressure on downstream systems. We can be more resource efficient if we send less data downstream (without sacrificing data quality).

The solution here was to simply sample in Logfwdr, in addition to maintaining the sampling in centralized receivers. How the sampling algorithm works here, in short, is each dataset has a key that producer teams have chosen to index and sample the data. When sampling, we first shuffle the records for each key to eliminate bias. Then, for each group of records, we select a sample size equal to the square root of the total count of the records. The result is a representative sample, whether sampled once or twice. To produce estimates, we scale calculations against the sample rate. For example, if we sample 10 out of 100 records, the sample rate would be 10/100, and the unbiased estimate of the original count would be 10*10 = 100.

To ensure this approach was working well, we compared the number of rows written to ClickHouse against the estimated sum for total count using a variety of keys across a variety of traffic footprints, so that “least seen” keys to “most seen” keys were captured across the spectrum.

The result is that for keys with more data, the sample rate decreases. However, keys with less data were sampled comparably. Thus, we still kept a representative sample while delivering and storing fewer events. We’re not compromising the quality of data delivered, even when we deliver less in quantity.

If we look at this more closely, using power laws, we can observe that the double-sampled (red) grows at roughly x0.319 v. sampled-once/control (blue) at x0.485. Another way to picture this is, a key that has 100x more data than another key would have stored roughly 10x the number of rows if single-sampled. Now, it will only store roughly 4x the number of rows. Concretely, a total of 11.6 million events is represented by 18k rows in ClickHouse as opposed to 79k. Double sampling attenuates storage of the “most seen” keys, while still retaining the same detail per event for “least seen” keys.

We initially implemented this strategy against three of our top datasets. Every single one at least halved the amount of compressed data we were originally sending on the wire to centralized receivers. That’s 25GB/s altogether, or over 2PB/day.

Aggregating

Cloudflare offers several analytics datasets built on rollups: aggregates of the raw events computed at ingest time. This makes the opposite tradeoff to sampling: rather than answering any question approximately, we answer a fixed set of questions exactly, provided we choose the dimensions and metrics up front.

For example, in the HTTP dataset, we measure the number of unique occurrences of IP addresses during a given minute rather than the individual IPs themselves. Another example is we sum the total number of GET, POST, PUT, etc. requests for a given domain, for that minute, grouped by the HTTP method. None of these computations actually necessitate waiting until the tail-end of the pipeline to start calculating.

Historically, this aggregation occurred towards the end of the pipeline, inside the inserters which read from Buftee and insert into ClickHouse. Decentralizing this aggregation was an opportunity to spread out load and reduce the amount of data we centralize.

Hence, we built an aggregation functionality that is utilized every step of the way, creating repeated opportunities to combine matching partial aggregates as data converges. Much like sampling, records are grouped by a key, which determines which records can be combined. We aggregate on each instance of Logfwdr. We aggregate again after the partially aggregated events reach the centralized receivers, which push these re-aggregated events onto dedicated partitioned buffers. Because these buffers bring together records from multiple receivers, we aggregate another time after they’ve been read in batches by the ClickHouse inserters. Finally, we aggregate in ClickHouse with aggregating table engines.

The first dataset we rolled this out to was for the HTTP traffic. In just this one dataset alone, we dropped from 9+ GB/s to <2 GB/s in compressed bytes traffic. Even though this is currently the highest cardinality dataset, the aggregations on it still gave us an approximate 80% reduction on the wire.

This aggregation feature is powerful for datasets that can collapse easily, especially for use cases like usage metrics where accuracy on the sums and counts is paramount. It also means we can offer producer teams another option to reduce resource usage besides sampling, which we did. Like Ready-Analytics, we created a generic in-house one-click aggregating analytics product, called Ready-Aggregates. As we continue to iterate on this new feature in the pipeline, we expect to see savings continue to mount.

Impact

The starkest proof of this exponential growth is how rapidly traffic growth consumes headroom.

Take Ready-Analytics for example, where two of the three mechanisms, load balancing and sampling techniques, were applied. In mid-May, load balancing dropped traffic by 50%, plunging from ~26 GB/s to ~13 GB/s. Two months later, traffic had already started surging back up to ~20 GB/s. That’s about half of the reduction, erased by organic traffic growth. We then created even more headroom by reducing this dataset’s throughput rate to the single digits, ~8GB/, when sampling rolled out.

Without both interventions, Ready-Analytics alone would have breached 60 GB/s by September. By processing less data in centralized data centers, we also save a significant amount of CPUs and memory. The following graphs show the impact of load-balancing and sampling in Logfwdr on the CPU and memory usage of just the Ready-Analytics receivers: a ~50% reduction, regaining ~750 CPUs and 3.5 TiB of memory.

Across the entire pipeline altogether, from spring to fall, load balancing (~38 GB/s saved), sampling (~25 GB/s saved across top datasets), and aggregating (~7+ GB/s so far), eliminated ~70 GB/s of compressed traffic from our backbone. These cliff drops provide immediate relief.

If we zoom out such that we look at five years from now, the changes made in this year alone have just as much impact as the short-term benefits. We’ve halved the amount of data we’d be processing in another half a decade’s time. The structural and algorithmic optimizations we have and will continue to make are essential to keep hardware demands sustainable.

If you’re interested in helping us solve these challenges at scale, we’re hiring!

entries.title: Filter, reshape, and redact logs before export with Transformers
entries.summary: Logpush now supports Transformers, allowing teams to filter, redact, and reshape log streams using SQL before export. Powered by Apache DataFusion and Apache Arrow, Transformers apply those changes directly to log data before it reaches the destination.
entries.content:
Logpush delivers logs in batches as quickly as possible, enabling Cloudflare to provide information almost in real time. During our recent Birthday Week, we made Logpush available on all self-serve plans and Transformers generally available.

Those changes were among eight major updates to Cloudflare Observability and reflect our commitment to make every Cloudflare feature available to everyone. This post takes a deeper look at how Transformers work inside Logpush's export pipeline. Observability teams use Logpush to export Cloudflare logs to security information and event management systems (SIEMs), analytics platforms, and object storage. Before those logs reach their destination, teams may need to remove health checks, omit sensitive fields, or reshape records for dashboards and investigations. Today, this often requires a separate processing service that teams must deploy, scale, monitor, and maintain.

For example, a team that collects logs from multiple CDNs can add a static provider field to normalize records before they reach its analytics platform. Teams also pay to export, ingest, and store records they discard as soon as they arrive, so filtering them before delivery can reduce downstream data volume and cost.

With Transformers, that processing moves into the Logpush export workflow.Teams define a SQL query to filter records, redact sensitive data, and reshape the output by adding, renaming, removing, or nesting fields. Logpush applies the query before export, so each destination receives data in the form it needs. We made this workflow simple for customers by embedding a SQL transformation engine in Logpush's high-throughput export pipeline while keeping performance and resource use predictable.

How Logpush Transformers work

A Transformer is a SQL query written for a specific Logpush dataset. The query references fields from that dataset and defines which records and fields Logpush should export. Logpush applies the query to each batch before export. Records that do not match the WHERE clause are removed. For the remaining records, the output of the SELECT statement becomes the exported record. Transformers can change the structure and contents of each record, and the transformed results are exported in NDJSON format.

Customers can create, preview, and manage Transformers in the Cloudflare dashboard through Transformer Studio or programmatically through the API. After saving a Transformer, they can attach it to a compatible NDJSON Logpush job that uses the same dataset. Each update creates a new version, so customers can review how a Transformer has changed over time.

The following example reshapes a Cloudflare HTTP request log to match a team-defined schema used across CDN providers. It does not convert between serialization formats: both the input and output use NDJSON.

      
{
  "ClientIP": "203.0.113.42",
  "ClientRequestHost": "example.com",
  "ClientRequestMethod": "POST",
  "ClientRequestPath": "/api/checkout",
  "ClientRequestUserAgent": "Mozilla/5.0",
  "EdgeResponseStatus": 502,
  "EdgeStartTimestamp": "2026-05-21T15:00:00Z",
  "RayID": "8e2a1c60ef9e1c9a"
}

The Transformer renames and nests fields, redacts part of the client IP address, adds provider and error information, removes unused fields, and filters out internal and health-check traffic:

      
SELECT
  extract(epoch FROM to_timestamp(EdgeStartTimestamp)) AS unix_ts,
  regexp_replace(ClientIP, '\.\d+\.\d+$', '.XXX.XXX') AS redacted_ip,
  UPPER(ClientRequestMethod) AS method,
  EdgeResponseStatus AS status,
  RayID AS ray_id,
  'cloudflare' AS provider,
  named_struct(
    'host', ClientRequestHost,
    'path', ClientRequestPath
  ) AS request,
  EdgeResponseStatus >= 500 AS is_server_error
FROM http_requests
WHERE ClientRequestHost NOT IN (
  'internal.example.com',
  'health.example.com'
)
  AND ClientRequestPath NOT LIKE '/healthz%'
  AND ClientRequestPath NOT LIKE '/metrics%'

The resulting NDJSON record uses the normalized schema:

      
{
  "unix_ts": 1779375600,
  "redacted_ip": "203.0.XXX.XXX",
  "method": "POST",
  "status": 502,
  "ray_id": "8e2a1c60ef9e1c9a",
  "provider": "cloudflare",
  "request": {
    "host": "example.com",
    "path": "/api/checkout"
  },
  "is_server_error": true
}

How Transformers executes SQL with Apache DataFusion and Arrow

Cloudflare's data pipeline ingests more than one billion events per second. Its Logpush delivery service, which we call Bufstream, delivers more than 110 million Logpush records per second to customer destinations. It runs across hundreds of Kubernetes pods, each claiming a time slice of data from Buftee, Cloudflare's distributed log-based in-house message broker. This model distributes work horizontally across Logpush jobs. Job volume follows a Pareto-like distribution: most jobs operate at lower volumes, while a small number of high-volume jobs process millions of logs each second. Transformers needed to meet the same operational requirements as the rest of Logpush: reliable delivery, high throughput, and predictable resource use without introducing additional failure scenarios into the export hot path.

Our initial prototype ran customer-defined WebAssembly Transformers in Cloudflare Workers, which provides globally distributed, isolated compute. However, invoking a Worker would insert a network call into the Logpush export path. That remote dependency could introduce transient timeouts and retries, reducing delivery throughput and increasing delivery latency.

We decided to keep Transformer execution in-process within our delivery service to prioritize reliability and delivery throughput. We evaluated several SQL execution engines and selected Apache DataFusion, which already powers Cloudflare Basin.

Apache DataFusion is a Rust query engine built on Apache Arrow, with a SQL planner and vectorized, columnar execution engine. In a benchmark, executing a prepared Transformer against a synthetic 5,000-row http_requests batch from a single Go goroutine took about 3 ms, equivalent to roughly 1.6 million rows per second.

Attaching a Transformer to a job adds CPU work to its processing path. Bufstream uses per-job transform parallelism so high-volume jobs can execute transform batches concurrently. Embedding DataFusion in Bufstream lets those batches use the service's existing delivery infrastructure, including its scheduling, batching, and destination controls, without introducing a separate transformation tier or network hop.

Choosing DataFusion meant connecting Bufstream, which is written in Go, to an engine written in Rust. The next challenge was moving typed batches efficiently across that boundary.

The final design of the in-process Transformer pipeline is shown in the diagram below.

From records to columns

Bufstream receives compressed Logpush batches containing Cap'n Proto records from Buftee. For a job with a Transformer attached, Bufstream decompresses the batch, parses the eligible logs, and builds a typed Apache Arrow RecordBatch before executing the transform.

Apache Arrow is a language-independent, columnar in-memory format designed for efficient analytics on modern CPUs and GPUs. It represents flat and nested data as typed, contiguous columns. Arrow IPC gives Bufstream and DataFusion a standard way to exchange batches across the foreign function interface (FFI) boundary between Go and Rust, exposed through a C application binary interface (ABI) and called from Go using cgo, Go's mechanism for calling C code.

The Go and Rust runtimes do not share ownership of transform data. Go passes a pointer to its input Arrow IPC buffer to Rust only for the duration of the cgo call, and Rust does not retain that pointer after returning. Rust owns the transformed output buffer; Go copies it into Go-managed memory and then explicitly releases the Rust allocation. This makes ownership and lifetimes explicit across the language boundary, avoiding cross-runtime memory-management bugs.

Using Arrow IPC means the Rust DataFusion wrapper can use an Arrow 

StreamReader
 to read typed 
RecordBatch
 values, rather than parse individual rows from an intermediate format such as JSON and rebuild typed Arrow columns for execution. Field types, nullability, and nested values are represented consistently on both sides of the boundary, so DataFusion receives data in its native columnar model.

Crossing the Go/Rust boundary is not free: batches still need to be serialized, decoded, and managed in memory. Arrow IPC keeps that work batch-oriented and avoids per-record parsing and conversion. This makes the boundary a better fit for Logpush's high-throughput delivery pipeline while retaining schema validation against the Logpush dataset definition.

Every Arrow batch needs a schema describing its fields and types. Rather than infer that schema from the logs in a particular batch, Bufstream supplies a generated schema from each Logpush dataset's specification. This gives DataFusion a stable view of the available fields and types, enabling query validation. The table named in a Transformer's FROM clause selects which dataset schema the query uses. For example, this Transformer queries the http_requests dataset:

      
SELECT ClientIP, EdgeResponseStatus, RayID
FROM http_requests
WHERE EdgeResponseStatus >= 500

Executing the transform

When a customer saves a Transformer through the API or Transformer Studio, Cloudflare stores its SQL query in R2. Bufstream retrieves the query through a multi-layer cache and translates it into a reusable DataFusion logical plan that defines the scan, filters, projections, and expressions. Bufstream prepares this plan once per time slice of a job's data and reuses it for every Arrow batch in that slice. For every new Arrow batch, the Rust wrapper binds the batch as the plan’s table input, executes the query, and returns Arrow batches containing the selected records and fields.

Transformers are designed to fail closed. If a transform cannot be executed, Bufstream neither advances the job's delivery offset nor sends the untransformed batch. Delivering raw data in place of transformed data could violate the schema, filtering, or redaction assumptions of downstream pipelines, so Bufstream opts to re-attempt failed transforms instead.

To prevent a persistently failing job from consuming capacity needed by healthy jobs, Bufstream progressively delays retries and reports errors on the job. Jobs that remain in a failing state for an extended period are automatically disabled. Customers can monitor successful and failed transformations, data volume before and after transformation, and transformation duration in the Transformer Health view of the Health tab in Logpush.

Returning to the export pipeline

After execution, Bufstream converts the Arrow output into NDJSON logs. It batches, gzip-compresses, and uploads those logs to the configured destination. Destinations accept data at different rates and can temporarily slow down. Bufstream adjusts the number of upload goroutines while respecting destination concurrency limits.

By embedding SQL execution in Bufstream, Transformers use Logpush’s existing distributed infrastructure, batching, and destination controls. Cloudflare’s data pipeline handles that complexity, while customers create and apply a Transformer with only a few steps.

Get started

Open Transformer Studio from the Logpush page in the Cloudflare dashboard and follow these steps:

  • Choose the Logpush dataset you want to transform.
  • Write your SQL query and preview it against a sample record.
  • Save the Transformer.
  • Attach it to a matching Logpush job.

Transformers is available on Free, Pro, Business, and Enterprise plans. See the Transformers documentation for setup details and the Logpush pricing documentation for current pricing information.

entries.title: Introducing Clef-omni with full multimodality, plus a faster Clef and a cheaper Clef-flash
entries.summary: We are expanding the Clef decision model family with Clef-omni, natively processing audio, video, images, and text in a single pipeline. We’ve also lowered Clef-flash pricing and boosted Clef inference speeds by up to 2.0x.
entries.content:
Following last week’s release of Clef and Clef-flash, Cloudflare’s open-weight decision models, we decided to bring forth more gifts. Today, we’re releasing Clef-omni, which takes in audio and video input alongside text and image. We also cut the price of Clef-flash so it is now cheaper than Jev, and we made Clef faster.

Although the model game is still early for Cloudflare, innovation and iteration is in our DNA, and we apply these principles to everything we do. In fact, the story of Clef came together over the course of less than a week. We decided we wanted to do something in the decision model space on a Friday evening, trained the model over the weekend, and launched it on Thursday. Even with such a short timeline, we were able to ship performant, high-quality, open-weight models for the community — imagine what more we can do in the future.

For today, we’re excited to keep up the momentum with new additions and improvements to our Clef family of models. This is just the beginning, and we’ll continue to get better, faster, cheaper, and more innovative.

Clef-omni takes audio, video, image, and text input

Our new Clef-omni model is able to take audio, video, image, and text input. This changes the paradigm for decision models, which have been largely text-only since the debut of Jev from TypeSafe. With Clef, we supported images and video frame arrays, but Clef-omni is able to take in audio (wav or mp3) and video (mp4 or webm) alongside text and images.

Instead of setting up cascading pipelines of models that transcribe speech-to-text, or splitting audio and image channels from video, you can just call one model to make decisions across any modality. We are now one step closer to a model that is able to interact with the world as we experience it — through audio, visual, and textual communication, all in one.

Check out our developer docs for the new Clef-omni model. We also released the model open-weights on HuggingFace. For a quick start, here’s how you can send new modality inputs to Clef-omni:

      
curl https://api.cloudflare.com/client/v4/accounts/$CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID/ai/run/@cf/cloudflare/clef-omni \
  -X POST \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $CLOUDFLARE_AUTH_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "model": "clef-omni",
    "state": "Review the installation: a photo of the unit, an audio recording of it running, and a video of the fan.",
    "images": ["data:image/png;base64,"],
    "audio": ["data:audio/mpeg;base64,"],
    "videos": ["data:video/mp4;base64,"],
    "questions": {
      "label_visible": {"type": "noul", "instructions": "Is the model and serial number label visible in the photo?"},
      "sounds_normal": {"type": "noul", "instructions": "Does the unit sound like it is running smoothly, without rattling or grinding?"},
      "fan_running": {"type": "noul", "instructions": "Is the fan running in the video?"}
    }
  }'

Clef-omni expands our open-weight decision architecture to natively handle multimodal workflows. We built this on a Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B-Instruct mixture-of-experts (MoE) foundation, where the model was already capable of processing text, imagery, audio, and video directly within a single pipeline. However, we adopt the primary comprehension backbone while discarding the text-to-speech output components. In production, Clef-omni executes a quick prefill pass across the complete payload, scoring all modalities and valid parameter options simultaneously.

Because we skip output token generation since Clef models are not Large Language Models (LLMs), we remove the overhead of transcribing or captioning incoming files. Media elements map straight into the unified sequence, where video and audio are synced with visual frames for joint processing. Clef-omni then pulls candidate values directly from internal embeddings using our two-stage attention routing: every valid option gathers key evidence from the input (regardless if they are buried in text snippets, visual elements, or audio streams) before field vectors cross-attend across the full context to compute confidence scores. We add a built-in lexical grammar that preserves option semantics, so that we can deliver fast, schema-constrained scoring across every input type.

We train the model with the same techniques as we did with Clef — freezing the Qwen3 backbone, training low-rank adapters (LoRA), and applying our standard post-training approach: combining label-smoothed cross-entropy loss with Brier score calibration. The result is a model that is resilient and designed to succeed regardless of schema variations, field ordering, and prompt structures.

This brings several core upgrades to the Clef model family. Calibrated, schema-bound decisions now seamlessly handle text, images, audio, and synchronized video in a single API call. It's also fast. Text-only decisions return in about 130 ms at the median, image inputs in about 150 ms, and audio clips in a few hundred milliseconds. Even a full 21-second video clip with sound is scored in about 1.5 seconds, all in a single API call.

Our benchmarking shows strong performance across benchmarks, even with new modalities and MoE architecture.
